489.name: Skell
489.province: the Abhainn naomh, above its mouth on the western coast
489.history: The greatest landing of the Old Ones lies a short way up the Abhainn naomh from the western sea, where the river runs broad and brown past a low bank of gravel and the tide pushes up against the current twice a day. Boats lay there long before the mole, pulled up on the gravel and dragged higher at every flood. The mole was begun by an old man who chose each boulder by its weight in his hands and set it with his grandsons standing in the river to their chests against the push of the water; it was laid out from the bank without mortar, stone set against stone, and in its first winter it held against a flood that took boats from every other stretch of that bank. After that the households of the river asked for the same lee and built beside it, and the landing grew on the mole's shelter as a village grows on a spring. By the time the Old Ones held every coast of the island, Skell was the one place among them that a stranger would have called crowded: some three hundred souls at the height, every mooring behind the mole taken, smoke from forty hearths lying along the river on a still evening. A woman of the landing walked the mole's length each evening at the turn of the tide, looking for any stone the current had worked loose, and the stones she reset were set the old way. When the heights were left and the households that had gone up to the rings came down, some came here, and one grandfather of the landing never once spoke of what he had seen up there. At the close of the age the mole stands whole, its foot under water at the lowest tides, and the landing keeps to the river as it always kept.
489.known_for: the mole of unmortared boulders, the eldest work on the Abhainn naomh

16.name: Skell
16.history: The least of the three Skells sits on the far north-western coast, on bare ground where no tree grows and the gales off the open sea come in unbroken across low heather and bog. Its few households fished the grey water below the horn and lived close to the shore under turf, until one household raised a round tower of dry stone on the rock above the landing, with a hollow wall and a stair wound up inside its thickness. A winter storm threw down the unfinished outer face in the second year of the building, and the household set it up again course by course the next spring, feeling every stone into its bed. The first night anyone slept at the tower's crown was remembered as a night of stars and no wind at all, which on that coast is a rarer thing than a stranded whale. The household walked the stair from foot to crown after every storm, feeling along both faces for a stone gone slack, and one night a fire lit on the parapet turned a boat from the rocks below. The tower looks out over the water where the Watcher was afterwards seen, and by the close of the age the households of the horn keep their boats out of that water as the hill-folk of the same coast do, each for their own reasons, neither knowing the other's. The landing holds a few dozen souls, the tower and some turf houses in its lee; nothing has ever grown taller than the tower there.
16.known_for: the hollow-walled round tower over the north-western water

132.name: Skell
132.history: The northern Skell stands on a wide bay of the north coast, facing the open sea that the island's northern shore takes square on its chin. Its households knew of the great mole on the Abhainn naomh by telling long before any of them had seen it, and when they came to build their own they made it shorter and curved against the swell, since a river's push and the sea's roll are two different weights. Each stone was laid dry against the course already set and worked back and forth until it sat without rocking, and only then bedded; a swell broke over the unfinished mole in its first autumn and moved nothing, which the households took as the sea's own leave to go on. The curved mole was finished in the lifetime of the grandchildren of those who began it. A traveller from this Skell who went the long way round to the western river and stood on the first mole came home saying the two were built the same way, stone by stone without mortar, and that the western one was the longer and the northern the harder to lay. In the years when the heights were left, a household that had lived within the three rings came down to this coast and learned to live by the tide again. At the close of the age the landing is a village of several hundred, its boats in the lee of the curve, and amber from the bay's strands is kept in its houses as a thing pleasant to hold.
132.known_for: the curved mole against the open sea

328.name: Brenn
328.province: the northern coast, west of the Toll dune
328.history: Brenn lies on the north coast where the rock shelves down into deep water in broad flat steps. Its households laid long ramps of flat stone from the shore into the sea, slab after slab, each one bedded on the one below and relaid where the sea shifted it; one slab was relaid twice before it held. When the first ramp was finished a dog of the household took to lying full length on it on warm days, and the household stepped over the dog on the way down to the water rather than move it. The ramps were wide enough for hulls greater than any hide boat, and on them the households framed the first plank-built hull on the island, launched it down the stone and watched it go out past the last shelf. A sail was seen small from the height above Brenn the next summer and not afterward. More hulls went down the ramps in the lifetimes after, and of them nothing is left, nor any telling of where they went; a second ramp was begun beside the first when the first could not serve the work. By the close of the age the ramps stand clean and pale at low water, green-slicked at their feet, and the households use them for their own boats, which are small. Some sixty souls live there, fishing the rock ledges west of the landing.
328.known_for: the stone ramps into deep water and the hulls that left them

37.name: Toll
37.province: the northern coast, under the dune
37.history: The northern Toll takes its name from the sea-caves under its headland, where the water booms at the turn of the tide. Its households raised a cluster of stone huts in the lee of a great dune, which kept the wind off them for a lifetime. Then a wind rose off the sea that did not settle for three days, and the household left the huts with what they could carry; when the wind fell the dune stood forward the whole width of the huts and beyond, a slope of new pale sand over ground where doors had opened two days before. No one dug for the huts. New walls were raised inland of the buried row within the season, and the sand has kept the old huts whole ever since, hearths, doors and all. The households of the new walls keep a strict eye on the dune's face and plant marram on its brow, and children are told early not to dig in it. At the close of the age Toll is a fishing landing of some fifty souls, living inland of the sand, with the caves below the headland for shelter from the worst weather and for the drying of nets.
37.known_for: the huts the dune buried whole

47.name: Bral
47.history: Bral sits on the far western coast at the foot of a cliff, where a strip of shingle gives on to the sea and the grazing lies above out of reach. For generations the households went up and down by a scramble no child could climb alone. Then a household set the first slab on the worst of the scramble, and after it cut steps into the rock itself, a few in a season, until the steps reached the first shelf, a third of the way up the cliff. Above the shelf the rock ran harder and gave up fewer slabs, and a worker might spend a season on a stretch that yielded three steps; an old woman used to sit of an evening on the shelf and run her hand along the edge of the topmost step then cut, saying of the rock above only that it would come when it came. It came. The two hundred and twelfth step was cut in her grandchildren's time, and the grazing above was reached by a stair. The lower treads, cut soonest and walked longest, wore a shallow dish into their middles before the upper treads had worn at all. Late in the age a chip of the coloured coal, still staining the shell about it, was thrown on the landing's midden; a household found it and kept it among its trinkets, a bright stone with no use. How it came to the western coast no one there asked. At the close of the age Bral is a landing of some eighty souls, going up and down its stair twice a day with the flocks.
47.known_for: the two hundred and twelve steps up the cliff, worn hollow

127.name: Vell
127.province: the western coast, among the dunes
127.history: The western Vell is a small landing on a coast of dunes and wide sand, where the fishing is good in autumn and poor in the late winter. Its households learned to put the autumn by for the lean months. A woman of the landing dug the first pit in the dune's flank, lined it with clay carried from a bank upstream and lidded it with a slab, and stored dried fish in it through a winter; the fish came out sound. She set her later pits a full body's length apart, holding that a pit dug too near another drew damp, and the households after her kept the spacing without asking why. A younger household once cut the lining clay out of turn and spoiled a season's store, and the landing kept the turns strictly after. The pits run in a line along the dune now, dozens of them, and some that were forgotten when a household died out still hold fish bones under their slabs. Late in the age the doors of the landing were turned from the sea toward the dune, for the wind. At the close of the age some forty souls live there on fish and the store-pits.
127.known_for: the clay-lined store-pits in the dune

64.name: Warr
64.province: the western shore of Loch chrom
64.history: Warr lies on the western shore of Loch chrom, behind a broad marsh of reeds that stood between the dry ground and the open water. Its households fished the loch and gathered mussels in the shallows, and crossed the marsh on a track of trodden reed that sank a little every year. A household first carried shell out onto the sunken track and found that it held a foot where reed would not; within a generation the carrying of shell was yearly work for every household, and the shell was crushed underfoot on a flat stone by the water before it was carried out, since crushed shell packs and whole shell slides. A flood of the reed-marsh in a wet year drowned the road's middle length and the households raised it again a forearm above the reeds. The road runs a little over a mile, white in the sun, from the dry ground to the water's edge, and a girl of the landing was the first to run its whole length at once without stopping. A family of the northern shore came once to see it, having heard of a road made of shells, and went home saying it was so. The road is kept as a household keeps a hearth: a stranger's foot on another household's stretch is not a thing lightly done. At the close of the age the landing holds some seventy souls.
64.known_for: the shell road across the reed marsh

238.name: Ros ruadh
238.history: Ros ruadh is a harbour of the hill-folk on a red headland of the north-western coast, the furthest west the hearths of the north shore reach before the bare horn. Its households fished and hunted seal on the open water west of the headland, going out in skin boats in the calm months and coming home heavy. A calm summer filled its nets as no summer had, and in that same season seven boats of Ros ruadh went out on calm water and did not come home: the first on a still morning, the second eleven days after from a different stretch of the same sea, and five more before the autumn, with no storm to blame and no wreckage found. The widows named what had taken them, and the Watcher entered the tellings of the shore by name for the first time. In the years after, the headland kept seven empty places on its shingle where seven boats had lain, and no household built on them. The hunters of the north-west afterward left the open water for the lee of the headlands and the strait, and Ros ruadh grew smaller. At the close of the age it is a landing of some thirty households who fish close inshore, keep an eye on the gulls, and do not speak of the water beyond the point after dark.
238.known_for: the seven boats lost in one calm season

1003.name: Crannagan Loch chrom
1003.history: The lake dwellings stand in the shallows of Loch chrom: platforms of split planks on piles of oak driven into the loch floor, joined to the shore by plank walks long enough to keep a household out of reach of anything that walks on four legs. The first platform was driven by a household that had cut the oaks on the shore above and floated them down, and the driving of a pile was work for every hand, the frame raised over the water and the weight dropped on the pile's head until it stood fast. A pile driven and holding was counted an occasion for a shared meal on the nearest platform once the driving-frame was struck down. Eels were first taken from beneath the platforms in baskets let down through the planks, and a child carried the first basket the length of the longest walk. Every morning a child was sent along the walks to listen for the sound of a plank gone thin under its light weight before a grown foot found it the hard way. Who built the platforms, the people of the shell road or some other people of those years, the tellings do not agree, and the households on the platforms do not trouble to settle it. At the close of the age some twelve platforms stand in the shallows, and a new pile is driven most summers.
1003.known_for: the platforms on oak piles and the plank walks

1011.name: Creag Ruadh
1011.province: the hill above the eastern shore of Loch chrom
1011.history: Creag Ruadh is the red crag above the eastern shore of Loch chrom, a steep hill of reddish rock with a shelf of good ground about its shoulder and springs on its south face. The hill-folk of the lake shore lit their first hearths there in the lifetimes after the lake dwellings were raised, coming west out of the high valleys with fire carried in a pot from hearth to hearth, and they took the crag for the view it gave of the loch and of anyone coming across the water. They were herders more than fishers, and grazed their beasts on the slopes below the crag and down to the reeds. What passed between them and the people of the platforms, or the households of the shell road on the far shore, no telling of the crag keeps: the crag's households say they watched the smoke of the platforms of an evening, and that was all. By the close of the age some eight or nine hearths stand on the shelf of the crag, lit from the mason's fire as every hearth of the hill-folk is, and their dead are laid in the ground below the red rock, facing the central mountains.
1011.known_for: its red rock and its view over Loch chrom
